1. Whoever acts unjustly acts impiously. For the nature of the universe has made rational beings for the sake of one another: to help one another as each deserves, and never to harm one another. So whoever goes against her will is plainly guilty of impiety toward the highest divinity. Whoever lies is also guilty of impiety toward the same divinity. For the nature of the universe is the nature of the things that exist, and the things that exist are bound up with everything that comes into being. Further, this nature of the universe is called truth, and it is the first cause of everything that is true. So whoever lies on purpose is guilty of impiety, because by deceiving he acts unjustly. And whoever lies without meaning to is guilty too, because he is at odds with the nature of the universe, and because he disturbs its order by fighting against the nature of the world. For anyone who is carried, of his own accord, toward what is contrary to truth is fighting against it. For nature had given him the powers to tell falsehood from truth, and because he neglected them he can no longer do so. And whoever pursues pleasure as good and avoids pain as bad is guilty of impiety as well. For such a person is bound to find fault with the nature of the universe again and again. He will complain that it hands out things to bad people and good people contrary to what they deserve, because bad people often enjoy pleasure and own the things that bring it, while good people get pain as their share, and the things that cause pain. Further, whoever is afraid of pain will sometimes be afraid of some of the things that are going to happen in the world, and that in itself is impiety. And whoever pursues pleasure will not keep away from injustice, and that is plainly impiety. Now there are pairs of things toward which the nature of the universe is equally disposed; for it would not have made both things in each pair unless it were equally disposed toward both. Those who want to follow nature should be of one mind with it about these things, and equally disposed toward them too. Pain and pleasure, death and life, honor and dishonor: the nature of the universe makes use of these equally. So whoever is not equally disposed toward them is plainly acting impiously. When I say that the nature of the universe makes use of them equally, I mean that they happen alike to the things that come into being one after another in a continuous chain, and to the things that come after them. They happen by virtue of a certain original impulse of providence. By that impulse providence moved, from a certain beginning, to the present ordering of things. Providence conceived certain principles of all that was to be, and it fixed the powers that would produce beings, and changes, and successions of that kind.

2. The happiest lot for a person would be to leave humankind without ever having tasted lying or hypocrisy or luxury or pride. The next best voyage, as the saying goes, is to breathe out your life once you have had your fill of these things. Have you decided to stay on with vice? Has experience still not persuaded you to flee from this plague? For the corruption of the mind is a plague—far more so than any such foulness and change in the air that surrounds us. The foulness of the air is a plague to animals insofar as they are animals; but the corruption of the mind is a plague to human beings insofar as they are human.

3. Do not despise death; be well content with it, since this too is one of the things nature wills. Think of being young and growing old, growing up and reaching full strength, getting teeth and a beard and gray hair, begetting, being pregnant and giving birth, and all the other natural processes that the seasons of your life bring: dissolution is just like these. So this is the attitude of a thoughtful person toward death: not careless, not impatient, not contemptuous, but waiting for it as one of the processes of nature. Just as you now wait for the time when the child will come out of your wife's womb, so be ready for the time when your soul will fall out of this casing. But if you also want a plain, ordinary comfort that will reach your heart, nothing will reconcile you to death better than looking at the things you are about to be taken away from, and at the character of the people with whom your soul will no longer be mingled. Not that it is in any way right to take offense at them; it is your duty to care for them and to bear with them gently. Yet remember that you will not be leaving people who share your principles. For this is the only thing, if there is anything, that could pull us the other way and hold us to life: to be allowed to live with people who share our principles. But as it is, you see how wearing it is when those who live together are out of tune with one another—so much that you might say: Come quickly, death, in case I too should forget myself.
4. Whoever does wrong does wrong to himself. Whoever acts unjustly acts unjustly toward himself, because he makes himself bad.
5. Often a person acts unjustly by not doing something, not only by doing something.
6. Your present judgment, grounded in understanding; your present action, aimed at the common good; your present state of mind, content with everything that happens—that is enough.
7. Wipe out the impression. Check desire. Quench appetite. Keep the ruling faculty in its own control.

8. Among the animals that have no reason, one life is shared out; among rational beings, one intelligent soul is shared out. In the same way there is one earth for all things made of earth, and all of us who have sight, and all of us who have life, see by one light and breathe one air.

9. All things that share in something common to them all move toward what is of their own kind. Everything made of earth tends toward the earth. Everything liquid flows together. Everything of the nature of air does the same, so that something is needed to keep them apart, and force has to be applied. Fire does move upward, drawn by the elemental fire above; but it is so ready to catch and burn together with all the fire here below that any material that is at all dry is easily set alight, because less of what hinders burning is mixed into it. In the same way, then, everything that shares in the common intelligent nature moves just as much toward what is of its own kind—or even more. For the higher it stands above all other things, the readier it is to mingle and merge with what is akin to it. So among animals without reason we find swarms of bees, herds of cattle, birds rearing their young, and something like love. For even animals have souls, and the power that draws them together is seen working in them more strongly, in a way never observed in plants or stones or trees. Among rational beings there are political communities and friendships, families and gatherings; and in wars, treaties and truces. And among things higher still, even though they are far apart from one another, a kind of unity exists, as in the stars. So rising to a higher level can produce a fellow-feeling even between things that are separated. See, then, what happens now. Only intelligent beings have now forgotten this desire and inclination for one another; in them alone this flowing together is not seen. And yet, though people try to escape this union, they are caught and held by it, for their nature is too strong for them. You will see what I mean if you only watch. So you would sooner find something made of earth that touches nothing earthy than a human being cut off entirely from other human beings.

10. A human being bears fruit, and so do God and the universe; each bears it in its proper season. And if ordinary usage applies the phrase 'bearing fruit' especially to the vine and the like, that does not matter. Reason bears fruit both for everyone and for itself, and from it come other things of the same kind as reason itself.

11. If you can, set those who do wrong right by teaching them. If you cannot, remember that kindness was given to you for this very purpose. The gods too are kind to such people; for some purposes they even help them to health, wealth and reputation—that is how kind they are. You too have it in your power to be like this; or tell me, who is stopping you?

12. Do not work like someone who is wretched, nor like someone who wants to be pitied or admired. Direct your will to one thing only: to set yourself moving and to hold yourself back, as reason, made for community, requires.
13. Today I got out of all trouble—or rather, I threw all trouble out. For it was not outside me; it was inside, in my opinions.
14. All things are the same: familiar from experience, lasting only a day, worthless in what they are made of. Everything now is just as it was in the days of those we have buried.
15. Things stand outside us, just themselves, by themselves. They know nothing about themselves, and they pass no judgment. What is it, then, that judges them? The ruling faculty.
16. The good and the bad of a rational being made for community lie not in what he undergoes but in what he does—just as his virtue and his vice lie not in what he undergoes but in what he does.
17. For a stone thrown into the air, it is nothing bad to come down, and nothing good to have been carried up.
18. Look deep into people's ruling faculties, and you will see what judges you are afraid of, and what sort of judges they are when they judge themselves.
19. Everything is changing. You yourself are constantly changing, and in a way constantly being destroyed; and so is the whole universe.
20. You must leave another person's wrongdoing where it is.

21. When activity ends, when impulse and opinion come to a stop—in a sense, when they die—that is nothing bad. Now think about your life: your life as a child, as a youth, as a grown man, as an old man. In these too every change was a death. Is this anything to fear? Now think about your life under your grandfather, then under your mother, then under your father. And as you find many other differences and changes and endings, ask yourself: Is this anything to fear? In the same way, then, the ending and stopping and changing of your whole life is nothing to fear either.

22. Hurry to examine your own ruling faculty, and the ruling faculty of the universe, and your neighbor's. Your own, so that you can make it just. The universe's, so that you remember what you are a part of. Your neighbor's, so that you know whether he acted in ignorance or with knowledge, and so that you also bear in mind that his ruling faculty is akin to yours.

23. Just as you yourself are one of the parts that make up a community, so let every act of yours be one of the parts that make up the life of the community. So any act of yours that has no bearing, direct or distant, on the common good tears your life apart and does not let it be one whole. It is a kind of mutiny—like someone in a public assembly who goes his own way and stands apart from the general agreement.

24. Children's quarrels and their games, and poor little souls carrying corpses around—that is what everything is. And so what is shown in the scene of the dwellings of the dead strikes our eyes all the more clearly.

25. Look closely at what kind of form a thing has. Separate it completely from its material, and consider it by itself. Then work out the longest time that a thing of that particular form is naturally made to last.
26. You have put up with endless troubles because you were not content with your ruling faculty doing what nature made it to do. But enough of this.

27. When someone blames you or hates you, or when people say something hurtful about you, go up to their poor souls, get inside them, and see what sort of people they are. You will find that there is no reason to trouble yourself about whether these people hold this or that opinion of you. Still, you must wish them well, for by nature they are friends. And the gods too help them in every way, by dreams and by signs, to get the things they care about.

28. The cycles of the universe are always the same, up and down, from age to age. Either the intelligence of the universe sets itself in motion for each separate thing that happens—and if so, be content with what its activity brings about. Or it sets itself in motion once, and everything else follows from that, in a way, as a consequence. Or indivisible elements are the origin of all things. In a word: if there is a god, all is well; and if chance rules, do not let yourself be ruled by chance too. Soon the earth will cover us all. Then the earth too will change, and the things that come out of that change will go on changing forever, and those in turn forever. For anyone who reflects on these changes and transformations, following one another like wave after wave, and on how fast they come, will look down on everything that perishes.

29. The cause of the universe is like a winter torrent: it sweeps everything along. How worthless they are, these poor little men who busy themselves with public affairs and imagine they are acting as philosophers! Drivelling fools, all of them. Well then, man, do what nature asks of you now. Get moving, if it is in your power, and do not look around to see whether anyone will notice. Do not hope for Plato's Republic; be content if the smallest thing goes forward well, and consider that result no small matter. For who can change people's opinions? And without a change of opinions, what is there but the slavery of people who groan while they pretend to obey? Come now, tell me about Alexander and Philippus and Demetrius of Phalerum. They themselves will judge whether they understood what the common nature required and trained themselves accordingly. But if they acted like heroes in a tragedy, no one has condemned me to imitate them. The work of philosophy is simple and modest. Do not lead me astray into arrogance and pride.

30. Look down from above on the countless herds of human beings, their countless ceremonies, their endlessly varied voyages in storm and calm, and the differences among those who are born, who live together, and who die. Consider too the life that others lived long ago, and the life of those who will live after you, and the life lived now among foreign peoples. Consider how many do not even know your name, and how many will soon forget it, and how those who are perhaps praising you now will very soon be blaming you. And consider that neither a name after death is worth anything, nor reputation, nor anything else.

31. Toward what comes from the cause outside you, let there be freedom from disturbance. In what you do from the cause within you, let there be justice. That is, let your impulse and your action end in this—in acts that serve the community; for this is in keeping with your nature.

32. You can clear out of your way many of the useless things that disturb you, for they exist entirely in your opinion. And then you will make plenty of room for yourself: by taking in the whole universe with your mind, by contemplating the eternity of time, and by observing how quickly each separate thing changes—how short the time is from birth to dissolution, how boundless the time before birth, and how equally endless the time after dissolution!

33. Everything you see will soon perish, and those who watched it perish will very soon perish too. And the one who dies in extreme old age will end up in the same state as the one who died before his time.

34. What are these people's ruling faculties like? What sort of things are they busy with? For what sort of reasons do they love and honor? Picture their poor souls laid bare. When they think their blame does harm or their praise does good—what an idea!

35. Loss is nothing but change. And the nature of the universe delights in change. In obedience to her, all things are done well now; they have been of the same form from eternity, and they will be so through endless time. What, then, are you saying? That all things have been bad and always will be bad? That among so many gods no power has ever been found to set these things right, and the world has been condemned to be bound in evils that never end?

36. The rottenness of the matter that underlies everything! Water, dust, bones, filth. Or again: marble, the calluses of the earth; gold and silver, its sediments; clothes, just bits of hair; purple dye, blood; and everything else is of the same kind. And the breath that is part of us is also another thing of the same kind, changing from this into that.

37. Enough of this wretched life, this grumbling, these monkey tricks! Why are you disturbed? What is new in this? What is unsettling you? Is it the form of the thing? Look at it. Or is it the matter? Look at it. Beyond these there is nothing. So toward the gods, now at last, become simpler and better. It is all the same whether we study these things for a hundred years or for three.
38. If someone has done wrong, the harm is his own. But perhaps he has not done wrong.

39. Either all things come from one intelligent source and come together as in one body—and then the part ought not to find fault with what is done for the good of the whole. Or there are only atoms, and nothing but mixing and scattering. So why are you disturbed? Say to your ruling faculty: Are you dead? Are you corrupted? Are you playing the hypocrite? Have you become a beast? Do you herd and graze with the rest?

40. Either the gods have no power, or they have power. If they have no power, why do you pray to them? But if they do have power, why not pray for them to give you the ability not to fear any of the things you fear, or not to desire any of the things you desire, or not to be pained by anything—rather than praying that this or that should not happen, or should happen? For surely, if they can help human beings at all, they can help them with this. But perhaps you will say that the gods have put these things in your power. Well then, is it not better to use what is in your power like a free person than to long, like a cringing slave, for what is not in your power? And who told you that the gods do not help us even with the things that are in our power? Start praying for such things, then, and you will see. One man prays: How can I sleep with that woman? You pray: How can I stop wanting to sleep with her? Another prays: How can I be rid of this? You pray: How can I stop wanting to be rid of it? Another: How can I keep from losing my little son? You: How can I stop being afraid of losing him? In short, turn your prayers this way, and see what happens.

41. Epicurus says: In my illness I did not talk about my bodily sufferings; nor, he says, did I discuss such things with those who came to see me. I went on discussing the nature of things as before, keeping to this main point: how the mind, while it shares in the movements that go on in the poor flesh, can stay free from disturbance and keep hold of its own proper good. Nor did I, he says, give the doctors a chance to put on solemn faces as if they were doing something important; my life went on well and happily. So do what he did, in sickness if you are sick, and in any other situation. For it is a principle of every school of philosophy never to abandon philosophy, whatever happens to us, and never to chatter idly with an ignorant person or with someone who knows nothing of nature, but to be intent only on what you are doing now, and on the instrument you are doing it with.

42. When someone's shameless behavior offends you, ask yourself at once: Is it possible, then, for there to be no shameless people in the world? It is not possible. So do not ask for the impossible. This person too is one of the shameless people who must necessarily exist in the world. Keep the same thought ready for the scoundrel, the untrustworthy person, and anyone who does wrong in any way. For as soon as you remind yourself that it is impossible for such people not to exist, you will become kinder toward each of them individually. It is useful, too, to think at once, as the occasion arises, what virtue nature has given human beings to set against each wrong act. For she has given us gentleness as an antidote to the stupid person, and against another kind of person some other power. And in every case you can set right, by teaching, the person who has gone astray; for everyone who does wrong misses his aim and has gone astray. Besides, how have you been harmed? You will find that none of the people you are irritated with has done anything that could make your mind worse; and what is bad and harmful for you exists only in the mind. What harm is done, or what is strange, if an untaught person acts like an untaught person? Consider whether you should not rather blame yourself, for not expecting that such a person would go wrong in this way. Your reason gave you the means to suppose that he was likely to make this mistake; yet you forgot, and now you are amazed that he has made it. But above all, when you blame someone as untrustworthy or ungrateful, turn to yourself. For the fault is plainly your own: either you trusted that a person of such a character would keep his promise, or, when you did him a kindness, you did not do it unconditionally, nor in such a way that you took all your profit from the act itself. For what more do you want when you have done someone a good turn? Are you not content to have done something in keeping with your nature? Do you want to be paid for it? That is as if the eye demanded a reward for seeing, or the feet for walking. For these parts of the body are made for a particular purpose, and by working according to their own makeup they receive what is their own. In the same way, a human being is made by nature to do good to others; so when he has done something kind, or anything else that serves the common good, he has acted according to his own makeup, and he has what is his own.
